title: SYSK Live: How Bars Work
summary: Live recording of Stuff You Should Know (recorded in Vancouver) on the history of bars and bartending. The hosts trace bars from ancient Pompeii hot-snack bars and Roman roadside inns, through Shawn's in Athlone, Ireland, and the founding of Gastown with Gassy Jack's bar, to the 1832 Pioneer Inn and Tavern law, election-day drinking and bumbo, and the New York bartending celebrities Erasmus Willard and Jerry Thomas (whose 1862 Bartender's Guide is discussed). The episode covers Prohibition and speakeasies, Canadian prescription liquor loopholes, the 1970s fern bar era with Henry Africa's, Dale DeGroff's return to classic cocktails, the origins of cocktails like the sling, Martini, daiquiri, Tom Collins, mojito and Caesar, and ends with a segment on Canadian whiskey (rye), the 1890 Canadian Club labeling law, and the Canadian Club "Hide a Case" campaign. Includes sponsor reads for Squarespace.

segments.title: Opening banter and bar origins
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter and introduce the question of when bars first appeared, noting that alcohol predates bars.

segments.title: Pompeii and Roman roadside inns
segments.summary: The earliest established bars are described in Pompeii, serving hot snacks and wine from counters. The Romans spread bars through inns along their roads.

segments.title: Shawn's in Athlone, Ireland
segments.summary: Shawn's in Athlone, Ireland is described as possibly the oldest bar in the world, said to predate the town built around it.

segments.title: Gastown and Gassy Jack
segments.summary: Gassy Jack built a bar within a day of founding Gastown in Vancouver. The hosts note the statue and the origin of his nickname, and mention older Victoria pubs.

segments.title: Hotel bars, bartenders as wealthy, and the 1832 Pioneer Inn and Tavern law
segments.summary: Bartenders were among the wealthy in tradition. Bars in hotels persisted, and the 1832 US pioneer tavern law let people drink without staying in a hotel. Industrial-age immigrants fueled neighborhood bars in New York.

segments.title: Election day drinking and bumbo
segments.summary: Bars were political centers, and candidates plied voters with drink; the rum punch called bumbo was used. George Washington lost his first legislature bid, then spent much of his campaign fund on booze and won. Some states still ban election-day drinking.

segments.title: Squarespace sponsor read
segments.summary: Sponsor read for Squarespace website builder with a free fourteen-day trial and promo code.

segments.title: Erasmus Willard and Jerry Thomas
segments.summary: Erasmus Willard, a celebrity bartender at New York's City Hotel, is described. Jerry Thomas, the flamboyant bartender known for the Blue Blazer, is introduced and his 1862 Bartender's Guide is discussed.

segments.title: Temperance, Prohibition and Canadian prescription loophole
segments.summary: The temperance movement led to Prohibition. In Canada, doctors wrote booze prescriptions; eight hundred and ten thousand were written in Ontario in one year. Speakeasies in the US outnumbered legal bars, and bad bootleg alcohol killed many people. Women began frequenting bars.

segments.title: Post-Prohibition pubs, tiki, and fern bars
segments.summary: After World War Two, pubs and sports bars spread in Canada and tiki culture in the US. In the 1970s, fern bars such as Henry Africa's in San Francisco brought ferns, Tiffany lamps and mixer drinks.

segments.title: Dale DeGroff and return to classic cocktails
segments.summary: Dale DeGroff was asked to set up a bar and was given the 1862 Bartender's Guide. He pushed for real ingredients and fresh fruit over mixers.

segments.title: Cocktail history: punches, slings, and classic drinks
segments.summary: Cocktails evolved from punches and toddies to slings; Jerry Thomas initiated the Baroque age of cocktails. The first cocktail was mentioned in print in 1803. Origins of the sour, fizz, daisy and margarita are touched on, and the hosts note the difficulty of Jerry Thomas's recipes.

segments.title: Martini, daiquiri, Tom Collins, mojito, and Caesar origins
segments.summary: The hosts discuss contested Martini origins (Martinez, California and Martini & Rossi), the daiquiri's invention in Cuba, the Tom Collins hoax, the mojito's pirate-era roots, and the Caesar from Canada.

segments.title: Canadian whiskey, rye, and Canadian Club
segments.summary: Canadian whiskey is called rye; its first distillery opened in Quebec City in 1769. A US law in 1890 required country-of-origin labels, which kept Canadian Club's name. The Hide a Case campaign hid cases of whiskey worldwide.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts note a missing listener mail segment and sign off with website and social media contact information.
